transcript.text: washing machine making a horrible noise

A horrible noise can range from an unbalanced load or a machine rocking on its feet, through a coin/bra wire or loose drum paddle, to a bearing or suspension problem. The type of noise and when it occurs will narrow it down quickly. 1. Switch it off and unplug it. With the drum empty, slowly turn the drum by hand. A light metallic tick or scrape once per turn suggests a trapped object or loose paddle; a rough deep rumble suggests bearings.
2. Press each top corner of the machine. It should not rock. If it does, levelling the feet may stop banging or walking on spin.
3. If the noise is a violent bang only with a duvet, bath mat, or one heavy item, redistribute it and try an ordinary mixed load instead—this is commonly just an imbalance. When does the noise happen—mainly on spin, while the drum turns during washing, or when it drains—and is it violent banging/shaking, a deep rumble, or a metallic ticking/scraping sound?
Mainly on spin, a deep rumble like a jet engine. Quieter during the wash. Got worse over a couple of months. Is it worth fixing?

It may be worth fixing, but it depends mainly on the machine’s age, overall condition and whether its outer tub can be economically dismantled. A deep, progressively worsening jet-engine rumble on spin is most often worn drum bearings. This is usually an engineer repair rather than a quick DIY job; on some machines it is a sensible repair, while on others the tub/drum assembly makes the labour cost too high compared with replacement. Before paying for a visit, do these two checks with the machine switched off and unplugged: 1. Open the door and turn the empty drum slowly by hand. Roughness, grinding or a gravelly feel strongly supports worn bearings.
2. Grip the inner metal drum at the top and lift it, then press each top corner of the machine. Noticeable up/down drum clunking points to bearings or the drum support; a machine that rocks on its feet may add banging, but would not normally create a deep roar. If the drum is rough or has play, avoid high-speed spins until it is assessed: continued use can damage the seal, tub or drum support. Get an engineer to quote for a drum-bearing/drum-support repair, then compare that quote with replacement rather than authorising work blindly. If the drum feels smooth and tight, levelling or suspension becomes more likely and is often cheaper to put right.
Ok did that. Drum rumbles/grinds when I spin it by hand, and there's a noticeable clunky up and down when I lift the edge of the drum.

That combination makes worn drum bearings the clear leading fault: the progressively worsening jet-engine rumble, grinding by hand and up-and-down drum play are the classic pattern. The bearing seal may also have failed, allowing the bearings to wear. A damaged drum spider/support is the other possibility, particularly if the drum has dropped or sits unevenly. It matters because an engineer needs to assess both before quoting; a spider fault can make the repair less economical than bearings alone. 1. With the machine switched off and unplugged, look through the door while slowly turning the empty drum. Check whether it remains centred with an even gap around it and does not rub the door seal. - Centred, but rough with vertical play: bearings are very likely. - Low/off-centre, visibly wobbling or rubbing: drum spider/support is more likely as well or instead. Avoid using high-speed spin cycles meanwhile. Continued use can damage the outer tub, door seal and drum support, which can turn a bearing repair into a much larger job. This is an engineer repair rather than a sensible DIY one. Ask for a diagnosis and quote for drum bearings/seal, with the drum spider/support checked at the same time; then compare the total against the machine’s age and replacement cost before authorising it.
Not sure how to tell, can't really see the gap properly. Machine is 9 years old, cost about £350 new. Is it worth getting fixed?

Probably not, on balance. For a 9-year-old machine that cost about £350 new, a drum-bearing repair is often uneconomical once labour is included—especially if the outer tub is not designed to come apart. The clunky drum movement also means the engineer would need to rule out the drum spider/support, which can make the repair poorer value still. The likely faulty part is the drum bearing and seal; the remaining alternative is the drum spider/support. The engineer suggests the distinction by dismantling and inspecting the bearing and drum support, rather than by the visible door gap alone. I would avoid paying for a repair unless you can get a fixed quote first and the machine is otherwise in excellent condition. Ask specifically for a quote covering drum bearings/seal, with the drum spider/support inspected before work is authorised. If the quote is a large share of a replacement machine, replacement is the sensible option. Until then, avoid high-speed spins and ideally stop using it: continued use can damage the tub, door seal or drum support and turn an already marginal repair into a write-off.
